summary: Describes how to build an IP echo host, which sends back IP datagrams after swapping the source and destination addresses. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: An IP echo host sends a datagram back to its original sender after changing its addresses. RFC 2075 explains how to handle special cases and reduce security risks.

how does an ip echo host work
what are the security risks of echo hosts
subtitle: How an IP echo host returns datagrams to their original source.

tldr.problem: Researchers need a way to test applications and protocols across network conditions without distributing prototype software to many test machines.
tldr.mechanism: An echo host swaps the source and destination IP addresses in a datagram, decrements its TTL, updates the header checksum, and sends it back.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes an Experimental service and warns about spoofing, loops, and flooding risks.

today: RFC 2075 is Experimental. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Echo Host
sections.content: An IP echo host returns IP datagrams to their original source with the source and destination addresses reversed, so the reply appears to come from the echo host. The RFC describes using this service to test applications and protocols across Internet conditions such as congestion, cross traffic, and variable round-trip times.
sections.plainLanguage: An echo host sends an incoming packet back to its sender, with the addresses reversed. This lets researchers test how traffic behaves across a network.

sections.title: Changing and Returning a Datagram
sections.content: For a datagram without options and whose protocol is not ICMP, the echo host exchanges the source and destination addresses, decrements the Time to Live (TTL) by one, updates the IP header checksum, and sends the datagram back. It must not echo a datagram if the TTL becomes zero or less. Datagrams with options may require additional changes; an incomplete source route must be discarded, while a complete source route must be reversed.
sections.plainLanguage: The host reverses the addresses and lowers the packet's TTL before sending it back. Some routing options need special handling, and an incomplete source route is discarded.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content: The RFC warns that a sender can use a forged source address to make an echo host send a datagram to a third party. It recommends that echo hosts SHOULD NOT be placed inside firewalls. Two echo hosts can also exchange spoofed datagrams; decrementing the TTL ensures each datagram eventually expires, but the RFC notes that many such datagrams can disrupt a network.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged source address can make the echo host send traffic to someone else. The RFC advises against placing echo hosts inside firewalls and explains that TTL limits, but does not prevent, flooding.
